title: China's Navy Passes 400 Ships, About 35% Larger Than the US Fleet by Hull Count
excerpt: Official US figures seen by the Wall Street Journal put China's battle force at more than 400 ships and submarines, with 71 major vessels added since 2020 — and US officials expecting Chinese submarines to operate routinely in the Indian Ocean by 2040.
body:
• China's navy now has a battle force of more than 400 ships and submarines, around 35% larger than the US Navy by hull count, according to official US numbers seen by the Wall Street Journal.
  • Beijing has added 71 major warships and submarines since 2020, 19 of them in the last year alone; the US fleet remains larger by tonnage and stands at roughly 290 ships.
  • On any given day, as many as 100 Chinese navy ships are out on Asia's busiest trade routes, with about half a dozen around Taiwan and roughly three times as many in the South China Sea.
  • US officials expect Chinese submarines to routinely operate in the Indian Ocean and Arctic approaches by 2040 — the timeline that matters most for India.

China now fields the world's largest navy by numbers: a battle force of more than 400 ships and submarines, according to official US numbers seen by The Wall Street Journal. That makes China's fleet around 35% larger than the American Navy by hull count. The US Navy remains ahead by tonnage — its ships are on average bigger — and America remains the benchmark for carrier operations, the Journal reported.

Built at shipyard speed

The buildup rests on China's shipbuilding scale: its yards churn out more than half of the world's merchant vessels every year and build warships at the same pace. Official US data shows China has added 71 major warships and submarines since 2020, 19 of them just last year. On Changxing Island across from Shanghai, satellite images from May showed two amphibious ships, two cruisers, three destroyers and two frigates under construction or maintenance at the same time, alongside the 40,000-ton Sichuan amphibious assault ship, dubbed a "drone carrier." A new class of submarine, likely nuclear-powered, appeared at the Jiangnan shipyard in June.

"They're not building a bunch of little corvettes. They're building a world-class navy."

— Thomas Shugart, former US Navy submariner, Center for a New American Security

Where the fleet operates

China has three aircraft carriers, with a fourth on the way that Western experts believe will be nuclear-powered, and a Pentagon report estimated it will have nine carriers by 2035, close to the US fleet of 11. Its core priority remains the arc from the Yellow Sea to the East and South China Seas — dominating those waters, absorbing Taiwan and blocking US intervention — but its deployments extend steadily outward, according to Times Now World's summary of the reporting. Beijing has also financed a network of overseas ports from Sri Lanka to Israel and Peru, and opened its first overseas base in Djibouti.

What to watch

For India, the consequential line in the US assessment is the submarine timeline: by 2040, US officials expect Chinese submarines will routinely operate in the Indian Ocean, Arctic approaches and possibly the Atlantic. China's president, Xi Jinping, told Communist Party leaders in 2013 that it was time to make the country a "maritime great power," and former head of US naval intelligence Michael Studeman told the Journal that Xi "fully believes... that any great power ultimately is a global maritime power." The US State Department said Beijing is using its maritime capabilities to project power and intimidate neighbours, and that the US will continue to uphold freedom of navigation alongside allies and partners.
